summaries.example: Imagine a school club where only one group gets to choose the activities, while another group must always follow. One person might say the problem is that choices and leadership are not shared fairly. Another might say the problem is the unfair rule that lets one group control the others. A third might ask how everyone could work together so that all members gain confidence and help make decisions.
summaries.summary: This entry explains several feminist ways of thinking about power. One view treats power like an important resource: if one group has much more of it, fairness may require changing how opportunities, respect, work, and decision-making are shared. Another view treats power as domination, meaning an unfair relationship that limits people. This domination can happen through a direct relationship, such as one person controlling another, or through wider social rules and habits. Feminist thinkers also ask how gender inequality connects with racism, class inequality, colonial history, and sexuality. Intersectional approaches say these forms of unfairness can overlap and create experiences that cannot be understood by looking at only one kind at a time. A different group of thinkers focuses on empowerment: power can mean building the ability to act, choose, resist unfairness, and work with others. The entry shows that philosophers disagree about the best definition, and that each definition may help us notice different problems.
key_ideas: Feminist philosophers study power because they want to understand and challenge unfair treatment connected with gender.
Some see power as a resource that should be shared more fairly.
Others focus on domination: rules, habits, and relationships that keep some people below others.
Some describe power as empowerment, or the ability to act together and help one another.
Power can work through direct commands, but it can also shape everyday rules, expectations, and ideas about who belongs in certain roles.
summaries.why_it_matters: The way we define power affects what unfairness we notice and what solutions we imagine. If we only look for someone giving orders, we may miss the effects of traditions, institutions, or expectations. If we only think of people as powerless victims, we may overlook their creativity, resistance, and ability to work together. Studying these ideas can help people ask fairer questions about rules, relationships, opportunities, and social change.

important_terms.definition: The ability to make something happen, or to affect what other people can do.
An unfair relationship in which one person or group controls, limits, or harms another.
The ability to act, grow, make choices, and help others become stronger too.
The idea that different kinds of unfair treatment, such as sexism, racism, and class inequality, can work together.

questions_to_think_about: Can a rule be unfair even when no single person is giving orders?
How might different kinds of unfair treatment affect one person at the same time?
What could it mean to use power with other people rather than over them?

summaries.example: Suppose a school offers leadership positions through an informal process. Teachers say the process is open to everyone, yet students who fit familiar ideas about confidence and authority are repeatedly chosen. A resource-based analysis might ask whether leadership opportunities are distributed unequally. A domination analysis might examine the norms and institutional practices that make some students seem naturally suited to lead. An intersectional analysis would ask whether race, gender, class, or sexuality changes how students are judged. An empowerment approach might focus on creating collective practices in which students develop authority without simply reproducing domination.
summaries.summary: The entry presents feminist philosophy as a field concerned with gender subordination, its connections with other forms of oppression, and possibilities for resistance and emancipation. It begins with a broad dispute about whether power is mainly power-over—getting others to act against their wishes—or power-to, a capacity for action that may never be exercised. Related theories ask whether power belongs to individuals, circulates through systems, or helps constitute people and social worlds. Liberal feminist approaches often treat power as a socially valuable resource that is distributed unequally. Critics argue that this picture can make power seem like a possession and can hide structural relations. Theories of domination instead analyze unjust power-over relations, but they disagree about whether domination is primarily dyadic, economic, embodied, discursive, colonial, or structural. Intersectional approaches stress that sexism cannot be separated from racism, class oppression, heterosexism, and other relations; critics debate whether intersectionality should be expanded, supplemented, or revised. Poststructuralist feminists analyze discipline, subject formation, norms, and resistance, while also facing questions about agency and political norms. Postcolonial and decolonial feminists challenge universal accounts shaped by imperial histories. Analytic feminists develop distinctions between individual and structural oppression and investigate how unjust systems endure. Finally, empowerment theories understand power as transformative capacity, collective action, or power-with rather than domination.
key_ideas: Feminist theories commonly analyze power as a resource to redistribute, domination to resist, or empowerment to develop, although these categories can overlap.
Power-over accounts emphasize control, resistance, and effects contrary to someone’s interests; power-to accounts emphasize capacity, potential, and collective action.
Power may operate through individuals, but systemic and constitutive theories also examine how social arrangements shape possibilities and even help form social identities.
Intersectionality challenges single-axis explanations by showing that gender, race, class, sexuality, and other relations can mutually shape experiences of subordination and privilege.
Poststructuralist approaches, drawing especially on Foucault, examine how norms and practices produce subjects while also generating possibilities for resistance.
Postcolonial and decolonial approaches warn against treating women’s experiences as universal and examine the links among colonialism, capitalism, racialization, and gender.
summaries.why_it_matters: Definitions of power are not merely verbal choices. They direct attention toward different evidence, subjects, and political strategies. A focus on unequal resources may support redistribution; a focus on domination may reveal hidden norms and institutions; an empowerment approach may highlight agency, solidarity, and collective transformation. The entry also shows why no single framework automatically captures every experience. Careful analysis must consider both individual action and broader structures, as well as the ways oppression and privilege can intersect.

important_terms.definition: A disputed philosophical concept whose meaning is debated because different theories emphasize different features.
Power understood as the ability to make another person do something, often despite that person’s resistance.
Power understood as a capacity or potential ability to act, achieve, or participate.
An account that explains power through individuals’ actions or abilities, rather than mainly through social systems.
An account that examines how institutions, norms, histories, and social arrangements shape people’s possible actions.
A theory that examines how forms of domination, such as sexism, racism, class oppression, and heterosexism, interact.
The capacity to develop agency and transform oneself or others without reducing power to control over them.
A view of gender and other social categories as shaped by social relations and practices rather than treated as fixed natural facts alone.

questions_to_think_about: Does fair distribution of opportunities solve domination, or can unjust structures remain even when resources are more evenly shared?
Can a person be both disadvantaged in one relationship and privileged in another?
If social norms help form our identities, how can people criticize and change those norms?
What does an empowerment-based theory gain, and what might it miss, compared with a domination-based theory?
How should feminist theories avoid speaking for people whose experiences differ from their own?

summaries.example: Imagine a student council where everyone is technically allowed to run for office, but the same kinds of students are treated as “natural leaders.” Some students also have less free time because they care for family members or work after school. One view would ask whether leadership chances and resources are shared fairly. Another would study the school’s rules, expectations, and traditions that shape who is heard. An intersectional view would ask how gender, race, and family income combine to affect different students. An empowerment view would ask how the council could help students build confidence and make decisions together.
summaries.summary: This entry surveys feminist debates about the meaning of power and how power relates to gender subordination. A basic disagreement concerns power-over, the ability to get others to do what one wants, and power-to, the capacity to act or accomplish something. Some theories focus on individual actions; others examine systems that distribute abilities unequally or help create social identities and social possibilities. Liberal feminist approaches often describe power as a valuable resource that should be distributed more fairly, along with goods such as work, prestige, security, and opportunities for development. Critics argue that this can treat power as a thing rather than a relation and can overlook institutions and structures. Theories of domination understand power as unjust subordination, but different traditions explain it differently. Phenomenological approaches examine lived bodily experience; radical approaches emphasize direct dominance; socialist approaches connect gender oppression with class and reproductive labor; intersectional approaches study the interaction of sexism, racism, class oppression, and heterosexism; poststructuralist approaches analyze discipline, norms, subject formation, and resistance; and postcolonial and decolonial approaches examine imperial, colonial, racial, and capitalist power. Analytic feminists distinguish individual wrongdoing from structural injustice. The final approach discussed is empowerment, which treats power as transformative ability, collective action, or power-with rather than simple control.
key_ideas: Feminist philosophers do not use one single definition of power; they compare several useful but competing approaches.
Resource theories ask how power and important social goods are distributed, while critics say power is better understood as a relationship or process.
Domination theories examine unjust control and include accounts focused on bodies, sexuality, economic work, social norms, institutions, and colonial histories.
Intersectionality rejects explanations that examine only one identity or form of oppression at a time.
Some poststructuralist theories say power does more than prohibit: it also produces norms, identities, and ideas about what is normal.
Empowerment theories describe power as the ability to act, resist, grow, and cooperate in ways that can increase rather than reduce others’ abilities.
summaries.why_it_matters: These theories help explain why equality is more complicated than giving everyone the same formal permission. A rule may look neutral while social expectations, economic arrangements, or histories make its effects unequal. Different frameworks also suggest different responses: redistribution, institutional change, resistance to norms, coalition-building, or collective empowerment. Learning the disagreements encourages readers to examine whose experience a theory highlights and what it may leave out.

important_terms.definition: Influence or ability that can be used to affect actions, decisions, opportunities, or social relationships.
Power used in an unjust way to control, restrict, or subordinate another person or group.
Power understood as a useful social good that people or groups may have in unequal amounts.
Power understood as a capacity to act, including the capacity to act collectively.
A relationship in which one person or group exercises control over another.
The idea that systems such as sexism, racism, and class inequality can overlap and shape one another.
The way social rules and practices can shape who people are and what actions seem possible.
The development of abilities, agency, and shared strength rather than control over others.

questions_to_think_about: Why might two philosophers define power differently and still both be studying something important?
Can power be widely spread through a society while domination remains?
How might everyday expectations shape people without anyone openly ordering them around?
Why is it risky to treat the experiences of all women as identical?
How could collective action count as power?
